classical

Liv. 5.47.4: clangōre eōrum ālārumque crepitū
Varr. RR 2.1.7: vōx eārum

eōrum, eārum

pronoun: genitive plural of is (eōrum masculine and neuter, eārum feminine)

their (someone else’s)

When the owners are not the subject: Manlius was woken clangōre eōrum, by the geese’s honking. It follows the owners’ gender: vōx eārum, the sheep’s voice.

Other words

  • suus, sua, suum — their (own), referring to the subject

    pronoun (possessive, reflexive), declension · classical · Liv. 21.58.8: tegminibus suīs magis obrutī quam tēctī; Liv. 21.28.1: cantūque mōris suī

    When the owners are the subject: the men lay tegminibus suīs … obrutī, buried by their own shields. The same word serves for his, her, its and their.

  • illōrum, illārum — their (those people’s)

    pronoun: genitive plural of ille · also used · classical

    For a stronger or contrasting “their”.

Examples

  • namque clangōre eōrum ālārumque crepitū excitus M. Mānlius

    for Marcus Manlius, woken by their honking and the flapping of their wingsLiv. 5.47.4

  • vōx eārum nōn mē, sed bē sonāre vidētur

    Their voice seems to sound not “meh” but “beh”.Varr. RR 2.1.7

  • nē, quās ibi posuerīs ad partum, nōn līberōs eārum, sed ipsās quaerās

    so that you aren’t looking for the snails you put there to breed, rather than their youngVarr. RR 3.14.1

  • tantum nivōsae grandinis dējēcit ut omnibus omissīs procumberent hominēs tegminibus suīs magis obrutī quam tēctī

    It threw down so much snowy hail that the men let everything go and lay down, buried rather than covered by their shields.Liv. 21.58.8

  • Gallī occursant in rīpā cum variīs ululātibus cantūque mōris suī, quatientēs scūta super capita

    The Gauls rush to meet them on the bank with all kinds of howls and singing in their own fashion, shaking their shields over their heads.Liv. 21.28.1

  • nostrī namque Gallī ventum ex suā terrā flantem, quem saevissimum patiuntur, circium appellant ā turbine, opīnor, ejus ac vertīgine

    For our Gauls call the wind that blows from their own land, which they find the fiercest, circius, from its whirling and turning, I think.Gell. 2.22.20

See also they, his, her, its, our, own.
